extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students and general readers studying American government/constitutional law
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook excerpt explaining limits on federal power, separation of powers, federal supremacy, interstate relations, and rules on citizenship and suffrage. Intended as descriptive guidance on constitutional doctrines and procedural protections under the federal system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of treason
rubrics_metrics.description: "Treason against the United States shall consist only in levying war against them or in adhering to their enemies, giving them aid and comfort."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Congress has no power to define treason beyond the constitutional wording; cannot vindictively declare acts treason that do not meet this constitutional definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safeguards in treason trials
rubrics_metrics.description: No person can be convicted of treason unless on the testimony of two witnesses to the overt act or on confession in open court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court in United States v. The Insurgents ordered juror names and witness lists be furnished and allowed reasonable time to prepare; until overt act proved by two witnesses no evidence relating to charges could be introduced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit on attainder and corruption of blood
rubrics_metrics.description: No attainder of treason shall work corruption of blood or forfeiture except during the life of the person attainted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevents the English practice where heirs lose inheritable qualities; punishment cannot forfeit real estate beyond the life of the traitor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on bills of attainder
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress cannot act as a court by passing a bill of attainder condemning any person to death, imprisonment, or imposing any penalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An explicit constitutional limitation to protect persons from legislative condemnations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on ex post facto laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress can pass no ex post facto law; i.e., cannot make an act a crime after it was committed, add new penalties after commission, or modify procedure to make conviction substantially easier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies to retroactive criminalization or punitive changes increasing liability after the fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warrants and probable cause requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal authorities have no power of arresting wholesale on general warrant; all warrants must be issued only upon probable cause supported by oath or affirmation and particularly describing the place to be searched and the persons and things to be seized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particularity and oath/affirmation are required to protect against general warrants and arbitrary searches/seizures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grand jury indictment and jury trial protections
rubrics_metrics.description: Indictment by grand jury and trial by jury are secured to all persons coming within the jurisdiction of the federal authorities, except in the insular possessions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guarantees procedural criminal protections in federal prosecutions (with territorial exceptions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Habeas corpus suspension limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The writ of habeas corpus cannot be suspended unless in case of rebellion or invasion, when it may be required by public safety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under ordinary circumstances any person held by federal authorities has the right to a speedy preliminary hearing before a proper judicial tribunal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excessive bail prohibition
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive bail cannot be demanded by federal authorities; except in capital cases, federal courts must release prisoners on bail and not fix amounts so unreasonable as to practically deny the right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protects against punitive or coercive bail settings that obstruct release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due process and criminal-trial rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal government must allow due process: trial open and speedy in the state and district where the crime was committed; defendant informed of the nature and cause of the charge; witnesses against him brought face to face; compulsory process for witnesses in his favor; cannot be compelled to testify against himself; right to assistance of counsel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collective enumeration of procedural protections forming core of criminal due process in federal prosecutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: State control over property definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: The power to define property is left to the state governments, subject to the one great restriction that slavery and involuntary servitude shall not exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Congress may define property in territories not organized as states and may define intellectual property under grants to authors and inventors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on duties on exports and apportionment of direct taxes
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress cannot impose duties on articles exported from any state; all direct taxes must be apportioned according to the population so that majority cannot shift the burden to the minority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protects interstate commerce and minority taxpayers; note exception for income taxes (historical caveat in text).

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformity of duties, imposts, and excises
rubrics_metrics.description: Duties, imposts, and excises must be uniform — must fall upon the same article with the same weight everywhere throughout the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensures national uniformity in indirect taxation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revenue bills originate in the House
rubrics_metrics.description: Revenue bills must originate in the House of Representatives, which is composed of members chosen directly by the voters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional protection intended to protect taxpayers by vesting origination in the popularly elected chamber (described as largely a dead letter in practice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriations required for withdrawals from treasury
rubrics_metrics.description: No money shall be drawn from the treasury except under appropriations made by law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevents executive withdrawal of public funds except pursuant to legislative appropriation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eminent domain and just compensation
rubrics_metrics.description: The federal government may take private property for public use but must make just compensation to the owner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In determining just compensation federal authorities must consider suitability of use, existing business or wants of the community, and reasonably expected immediate future; proceedings must be fair, afford opportunity to present evidence, and may be before commissioners or courts as Congress determines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of powers doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: Power conferred on the federal government must be distributed among three distinct departments: legislative, executive, and judicial — a doctrine embodied in the opening sentences of the respective articles of the Constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serves as checks and balances and subdivision of power to prevent tyranny by simple legislative majorities; historical origins from Montesquieu and English practice discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of powers not absolute in practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Framers understood complete separation was impossible; powers are shared (e.g., appointments and treaty-making shared with Senate; veto and messaging give President legislative role; Congress creates and controls departments and can affect courts by number/salaries).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes practical overlaps and possible legislative encroachments (e.g., through confirming power, creating courts, Tenure of Office Act example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial doctrine and limits on separation enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have been loath to hold acts of Congress invalid on the general theory of separation of powers; judicial application takes more precise forms as in Hayburn's case where judges refused non-judicial duties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separation doctrine is applied concretely to determine whether a power is 'judicial in its nature' and thus whether Congress may confer it on judges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critiques and defenses of separation of powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics argue functions are only legislative and executive and that separation creates friction; defenders emphasize independent judiciary and its supremacy in matters of private rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presents competing publicist views (Ford, Goodnow vs. Burgess) and the prevailing American view favoring independent judiciary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supremacy of federal law and role of Supreme Court
rubrics_metrics.description: "This Constitution and the laws of the United States which shall be made in pursuance thereof...shall be the supreme law of the land." Federal law is supreme and the Supreme Court is the final interpreter; its decisions bind Congress, states, and private persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains constitutional source and historical controversy resolved in favor of federal supremacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of federal officers exercising authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal officers acting within the scope of their authority must be protected from state interference; otherwise national operations can be arrested by a hostile state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by removal statutes and Tennessee v. Davis: removal to federal courts when federal duties are involved to prevent state obstruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal law can preempt conflicting state law
rubrics_metrics.description: State laws that violate principles of the federal Constitution may be set aside — federal constitutional law can invalidate state regulation (illustrated by bakeries hours case).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrates practical effect of supremacy in local regulatory contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privileges and immunities of citizens
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution secures to citizens of each state the privileges and immunities of citizens in the several states; federal judiciary defines and enforces them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Means certain great legal rights necessary to free migration, business, and property cannot be taken away from citizens of another state, but does not guarantee all privileges a person enjoyed in the former state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full faith and credit among states
rubrics_metrics.description: Full faith and credit shall be given in each state to the public acts, records, and judicial proceedings of every other state; authenticated acts shall be given the same faith and credit in federal courts as in the courts of the state from which they are taken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practically allows judgments and records (e.g., an Ohio judgment) to be enforced in another state (e.g., New York) without retrying the merits, subject to defenses like lack of jurisdiction or authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional extradition provision and practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person charged with crime, fleeing from justice and found in another state, shall be delivered up on demand of the executive authority of the state from which he fled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Congress has prescribed process; historically the governor's duty was viewed as moral rather than mandatory (Taney), and the extradition process involves formal demand with certified indictment/affidavit and gubernatorial action to surrender.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citizenship by birth (jure soli) and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: All persons born in the United States and not subject to any foreign power, excluding Indians not taxed, are ipso facto citizens of the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Children born abroad to citizen fathers may be deemed citizens under statute, but rights do not descend to children whose fathers never resided in the United States.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collective naturalization on territorial transfer
rubrics_metrics.description: Collective naturalization may occur when a foreign territory and its inhabitants are transferred to the United States; the manner is generally stipulated in the treaty of transfer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Louisiana purchase treaty terms for incorporation and admission to enjoy rights and immunities of U.S. citizens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional control and courts for naturalization
rubrics_metrics.description: The process of naturalizing individuals is subject in all details to the laws of Congress and is committed to certain specified courts (circuit/district or certain state courts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under supervision of Bureau of Naturalization; about 3,500 courts historically could issue naturalization papers under the 1906 law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Racial restrictions historically in naturalization law
rubrics_metrics.description: Only white persons and persons of African descent may be naturalized; Chinese excluded by law and exclusion extended to Japanese on racial grounds (historical text).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reflects historical statutory restrictions and judicial practice of the period; indicates legal discrimination in naturalization rules at that time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-stage naturalization procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Naturalization process: (1) declaration of intention at least two years prior to admission (applicant at least 18), (2) petition for citizenship 2–7 years after declaration and after five years' residence, with affidavits of two citizens certifying residence and good moral character, (3) hearing after ninety days where applicant is examined and judge must be satisfied of compliance, good moral character, attachment to the Constitution; certificate issued when court satisfied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges have large discretion; examination may be formal or thorough; instances of abuse cited when judges opposed to applicants' political principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: State control of suffrage under original Constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: The original Constitution left the right to vote to the states, stipulating voters for House members should have qualifications requisite for electors of the most numerous branch of the state legislature, and allowing states to decide how presidential electors are chosen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Did not create a national suffrage; after the Civil War Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments were pushed to protect freedmen's voting rights but did not create one uniform national suffrage — regulation remains with states subject to constitutional limits.
